div.head: ECf 32 E 3
div.ab: Impetrauit enim temporibus illis Arturus rex a domino papa et a curia Romana, quod confirmata fuit Norwegia imperpetuum corone Britannie in augmentum regni huius; uocauitque illam predictus Arturus cameram Britannie. Hac uero de causa dicunt Norwegienses, se debere in regno isto cohabitare, et dicunt, se esse de corpore regni huius, scilicet de corona Britannie.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 660 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

This passage is not part of ECf or ECf retr: it is one of the additions of the London collection (Leges Anglorum s. XIII in. Londoniis collectae), which Liebermann prints across the page as an insertion into ECf retr. 32 (32 A–E, pp. 655–660). The dictionary cites it as “ECf 32 E …”, so it is kept with ECf here.

note.seg: vielleicht angeregt durch päpstliche Bestätigung der Englischen Annexion Irlands 1172
perhaps prompted by the papal confirmation of the English annexation of Ireland in 1172
widerspricht sterilis 32 E 4. Vgl. Chanson de Roland 2332: Jo cunquis Guales, Escoce, Islande et Engleterre, que il teneit sa cambre
contradicts sterilis at 32 E 4. Cf. Chanson de Roland 2332: Jo cunquis Guales, Escoce, Islande et Engleterre, que il teneit sa cambre

seg.hi: statt den Besitz der Nordleute am Englischen Boden aus Englands Niederlage zu erklären, verkehrt der Londoner die Geschichte ins Gegentheil und vermengt weiterhin Aufenthaltsrecht fremder Händler mit der Nordischen Besiedlung Nordost-Englands

note.seg: instead of explaining the Northmen’s possession of English soil from England’s defeat, the Londoner turns history upside down, and further confuses the right of residence of foreign traders with the Norse settlement of north-east England

div.ab: For in those times King Arthur obtained from the lord pope and from the Roman curia that Norway was confirmed in perpetuity to the crown of Britain, for the enlargement of this kingdom; and the aforesaid Arthur called it the chamber of Britain. For this reason the Norwegians say that they ought to live together in this kingdom, and they say that they are of the body of this kingdom, namely of the crown of Britain.
